one_liner: Erlang/BEAM processes pass a token round a 503-member ring about 10x faster than a Boost.Asio C++ program using 503 OS threads.
what_it_does: This is a language-level data point, not a library. The thread-ring task from the Computer Language Benchmarks Game links 503 concurrent agents in a ring and passes one integer token 5,000,000 times. The Erlang program (Jiri Isa's Benchmarks Game submission, in scottgw/quicksilver) spawns 503 BEAM processes and uses plain `Pid ! Token - 1` / `receive`. The C++ program it is compared with (The Anh Tran's Benchmarks Game submission) creates 503 pthreads that all block in one boost::asio::io_service::run(), and every pass is an io_service::post().
how_it_is_fast: The speedup comes from green threads against OS threads. An Erlang process is a heap-allocated BEAM object, and a send-and-receive between two processes is a mailbox enqueue plus a user-space scheduler switch inside one runtime thread. In the C++ program each post() locks the shared io_service queue and wakes one of the 503 sleeping OS threads, so every pass costs a futex wake-up and a kernel context switch, often across cores. The task is essentially single-threaded (one token in flight), so the per-switch cost decides the result. The paper itself says thread-ring and condition test context-switching overhead.
when_to_use: Designs with very many mostly idle concurrent agents (thousands to millions of actors or sessions) that hand small messages to each other, where per-message cost is dominated by switching rather than computation.
Message-passing pipelines or rings where one OS thread per agent would be the natural C++ design and the C++ team would not otherwise reach for fibers or an executor.
Systems that also want BEAM's preemptive per-process scheduling, per-process heaps and supervision, with context-switch-bound hand-offs as a performance bonus.
As a reference point when arguing that an OS-thread-per-agent C++ design is the problem: the 10x gap measures thread models, not compilers.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Erlang beats C++ on concurrency in general: in the same paper's concurrent suite C++/TBB has the best geometric mean (1.57 s) and Erlang one of the worst (5.01 s, only Haskell is slower at 12.20 s), per a search summary of the paper.

Against a C++ design that uses user-space switching (Boost.Fiber, Boost.Context, C++20 coroutines on one executor, or a plain single-threaded loop); none was measured, and these remove the OS context switch that the C++ baseline pays on every pass.
CPU-bound kernels or numeric code: BEAM's single-thread compute is slower than optimised C++, and the 2014 run used the bytecode interpreter (erlc without +native, before the OTP 24 JIT).
Code that must call C on the hot path: NIFs or ports add a boundary and long-running NIFs block a scheduler.

integration.form: language runtime (Erlang/OTP: erlc compiler plus the BEAM virtual machine started with erl)
integration.dependencies: Erlang/OTP runtime (ERTS); the C++ baseline needs Boost.Asio and libboost_system
integration.min_toolchain: Not stated for the 2014 run (erlc -W, erl -smp enable); current master is OTP 30.0-rc0. The run script's -smp and +K flags no longer appear in the current erl command reference, so a modern rerun should drop them.
integration.platforms: Wherever ERTS runs (Linux, macOS, Windows, BSDs); the measured run was Linux on a 32-core machine whose CPU model was not seen
integration.thread_safety: Erlang processes share nothing and communicate by copying messages; the runtime runs one scheduler thread per logical CPU by default (+S).

gotchas: The C++ baseline in this comparison is not TBB and is not tuned for this task. It is the Benchmarks Game Boost.Asio program on 503 OS threads. Its claimed 4 KB stacks are not used on glibc either: pthread_attr_setstack() rejects sizes below PTHREAD_STACK_MIN (16384 bytes in glibc's Linux pthread_stack_min.h; check_stacksize_attr returns EINVAL), main.cpp ignores the return value, and the 503 threads get default-sized stacks. This harness flaw does not change the timing much, but the record's '503 OS pthreads (4 KB stacks)' should read 'default-sized stacks'.

The timers differ. In benchmarks/run_all.py, Erlang's TotalTime is its own timer:tc figure printed to stderr, which excludes VM start-up and shutdown. C++ is timed as wall clock around Popen (sh, run.sh, process launch and creation of 503 pthreads). Against 3.30 s and 34.13 s this is small, but it favours Erlang.

The thread counts are not equal. At HEAD, run_all.py runs the concurrent tasks only with workers = 4. Go's run.sh sets GOMAXPROCS=4. The C++ thread-ring ignores the worker argument (always 503 threads). Erlang's run.sh passes '+P 5000000 4', so the 4 becomes a stray plain argument, and BEAM starts its default of one scheduler per logical CPU. The '32 cores' attached to Table 5 may come from the parallel-task figure caption (Figure 18), so the published configuration is uncertain.

The paper numbers (Erlang 3.30 s against C++ 34.13 s) were seen only through WebSearch summaries; arxiv.org could not be resolved from this environment, and the repo has no result CSVs, so the table was not checked directly.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: This is the same paper and harness as the Go goroutines thread-ring sibling: Erlang is 3.30 s against Go's 13.98 s, so pick it if a context-switch-bound ring or pipeline is the whole workload. The GHC lightweight-threads sibling (skynet) measures spawn cost rather than hand-off cost, and Pony against CAF compares actors with C++ actors rather than with OS threads, which makes the Pony entry the fairer actor-runtime comparison.
verified_claims_summary: In West, Nanz and Meyer's ESEC/FSE 2015 paper (arXiv 1405.7153), the thread-ring entry in Table 5, seen through search summaries only, shows Erlang at 3.30 s against 34.13 s for the column labelled C++/TBB, about 10.3x (derived from those numbers). The C++ column is the Benchmarks Game Boost.Asio program (g++ -O3 -std=c++11 -pthread) on 503 OS threads. Erlang was plain BEAM bytecode from circa 2014. The run was on a Linux machine with 32 cores; CPU model and compiler versions were not stated, and the token was passed 5,000,000 times.
status_note: Erlang/OTP is actively maintained (Apache-2.0, 12.4k stars, master at OTP 30.0-rc0). The benchmark harness (scottgw/quicksilver, 2014) is unmaintained but public. Treat the result as a measurement of green threads against OS threads, not a reason to port C++ code to Erlang; the thread-count and timer mismatches and the misdescribed 4 KB C++ stacks are harness flaws documented above.
